title: Starship Mars Program Review
summary: Program review for the late-2026 Mars transfer window. The team locked the ship count at five uncrewed Starships, moved the propellant transfer demo to Flight 14, froze the Optimus payload configuration for August 15, and flagged heat shield tile attrition and Pad B turnaround as the two critical risks.
decisions: Commit to five uncrewed Starships for the November 2026 Mars window, down from seven
Fly the full ship-to-ship propellant transfer demo on Flight 14, not Flight 13
Freeze the Optimus Mars payload configuration on August 15
Move two Raptor 3 production lines to a three-shift schedule through October

action_items.task: Deliver the tile attrition root-cause report with the ceramic matrix samples from Flight 11
Get FAA sign-off timeline for Pad B dual-launch cadence in writing
Review and sign the Optimus payload freeze spec with the Tesla team

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Okay, Mars window review. We have roughly one hundred and twenty days until the window opens. Gwynne, where are we on ship count, honestly?

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: Honestly? Seven ships was always aspirational. We have four ships in final integration at Starfactory, a fifth in section stacking, and ships six and seven exist mostly as ring sections and optimism.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I'd rather fly five ships that all make it than seven where two break up on entry. Mars entry is the whole game. What's the constraint — Raptors or tiles?

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Tiles. Raptor 3 line is actually ahead of plan, we're at fourteen engines a week. The problem is we lost about eight percent of tiles on Flight 11 during entry, mostly on the windward flap joints, and Mars entry is a harsher thermal pulse than Earth return.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Eight percent is way too high. What was it on Flight 10?

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Three percent. The difference is we switched tile suppliers for the flap joint sections to hit rate. The new ceramic matrix batch has microcracking under thermal cycling. We caught it in the post-flight scans.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: So we traded reliability for rate. That's the classic mistake. The best part is no part, but the second best part is the part that doesn't fall off the ship.

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: We can revert the flap joints to the original supplier for all five Mars ships. It costs us about two weeks of tile installation schedule, which we can absorb if we drop from seven ships to five. That's actually the argument for five.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Fine. Five ships, old supplier on all critical zones. Done, decided. Mark, I want the root-cause report on the microcracking with actual samples on my desk in a week. If the supplier has a fix, I want to see coupon test data, not slides.

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: You'll have it by the 27th. We already have the Flight 11 recovered sections in the lab in Hawthorne.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Good. Now refueling. Every Mars ship needs roughly ten tanker flights. Five ships means fifty tanker launches in maybe ninety days. Walk me through how that isn't fantasy.

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: It's not fantasy but it's tight. It requires Pad A and Pad B both running, roughly a launch every thirty-six hours between them at peak. Pad B is licensed for the cadence but the FAA sign-off on dual-launch operations — both pads active in the same twelve-hour window — is still verbal, not written.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Verbal doesn't count. I've been burned by verbal. Get it in writing.

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: Already scheduled — I'm in DC on the 29th with their licensing team. I'll have a written timeline by end of month. Worst case, they want a supplemental noise assessment for the dual window, which is a six-week delay on the paperwork, not on flying.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Okay. And the transfer demo itself. We've done the settling burn and ullage transfer on Flight 12 but not full ship-to-ship. When?

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Plan of record says Flight 13, but I want to move it to Flight 14. The docking adapter quick-disconnect failed two of nine cryo cycles in ground test last week. It's a seal design issue, we have a fix, but it needs a requal campaign and Flight 13 is five weeks out.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: What failed exactly? The seal extrudes under cryo shock?

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Yes — the spring-energized seal loses preload below ninety kelvin on the liquid oxygen side. The fix is a different jacket material plus a preload shim. We've got the redesigned units in cryo cycling now, twenty cycles in, zero leaks.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Run it to two hundred cycles. If it survives two hundred, fly it on 14. I don't want to fly a demo that fails and gives everyone a reason to say Mars slips to 2028. The demo has to work the first time.

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: Agreed, and moving it to 14 doesn't actually threaten the window. The tanker campaign doesn't start until mid-September regardless. What threatens the window is Pad B turnaround. We're at four days between launches on Pad A. Pad B has never done better than nine.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Why is Pad B slow? Same hardware.

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: Newer crew, and the deluge system on B has a slower recycle — the water tanks are shared with the flame trench cooling loop, so we can't refill both in parallel. There's a plumbing mod that decouples them. Three weeks of work, and I'd rather do it in August than discover it in October.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Do it in August. Take Pad B down for three weeks starting the 10th, that still leaves buffer. Okay — payload. The whole point of this window is Optimus on Mars. Where are we on the payload freeze?

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Tesla side is iterating too fast, that's the actual problem. Every two weeks there's a new hand, new battery pack, new mass number. Current payload spec says ten Optimus units per ship plus the solar deployment kit and the Starlink relay package, but the mass keeps creeping. We're up six hundred kilos from the May spec.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: That's my fault, I keep approving the upgrades. Okay, hard freeze August 15. Whatever Optimus config exists on August 15 is what flies. I'll sign the freeze spec myself so there's no ambiguity about who said no to the next upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: Thank you. And to be clear about mission success criteria — I want us all saying the same thing publicly. Success for this window is ships landing intact and at least one Optimus walking off a ship and surviving a night. It is not a base, it is not propellant production.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Agreed. If one robot walks on Mars and phones home, that's the most important photograph since Earthrise. Everything else is bonus. What's our landing site status?

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Arcadia Planitia, the flat site we picked for ice access. We have thirty-centimeter imagery from the reconnaissance pass and the terrain relative navigation maps are built. The open question is landing dispersion — with no ground infrastructure, we're predicting a two-kilometer ellipse per ship.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Two kilometers is fine for this window. The ships don't need to be next to each other, they need to be upright. What's the biggest thing that keeps you up at night, Mark? Actual answer.

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Entry. We have exactly zero flights of Mars entry data. The aero database is all CFD and Earth-entry extrapolation. Mars atmosphere is thin enough that the flap authority margins are half what we have on Earth return. If the real atmosphere is off from the model on a dusty day, we could run out of control authority.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Which is why we're sending five. Ships one and two are honestly instrumentation missions with cargo. If we lose one on entry, the telemetry from that loss is worth the ship. I want every ship instrumented like a flying wind tunnel — full pressure taps, full thermal mapping.

transcript.speaker: Mark Juncosa
transcript.text: Already in the plan, about two hundred kilos of instrumentation per ship. That's part of the mass creep, for what it's worth. That part I'm not cutting.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Don't cut it. Cut a robot before you cut the sensors. Gwynne, budget line — where does the campaign land?

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: All-in for the five-ship campaign including tankers, we're at roughly two point one billion. That's inside the envelope the board approved in March, and Starlink cash flow covers it without touching the raise. I'll flag if the tanker count grows — every extra ten tankers is about ninety million.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Fine. And Artemis — NASA is going to ask whether Mars is stealing resources from the lunar lander. What do we tell them?

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: The truth — separate ship line, separate team, and the Mars tanker campaign actually retires the refueling risk that Artemis needs anyway. Every tanker flight this fall is a rehearsal for their mission. I've got a call with the administrator's office Thursday, I'll walk them through it before it becomes a headline.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Good framing. Okay, recap. Five ships, tile supplier reverted, transfer demo on Flight 14 pending two hundred cryo cycles, Pad B plumbing mod in August, Optimus freeze August 15 with my signature, and Gwynne gets the FAA dual-launch approval in writing. Anything I missed?

transcript.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
transcript.text: One thing. You have the all-hands Friday. The team is grinding hard and half of them think the window is going to slip because they read it on X. It would help if you stood up and said the window is real and five ships is the plan.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I'll do it Friday. And I'll stop tweeting ship counts until we've flown the demo. Probably. Okay, back to work — this is the most important thing any of us will ever do. Let's not blow it on a seal.
